error_modes.label: NAVIGATION ROUTE PLANNING AND ENERGY PLAN

texts.0: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, did not plan the navigation sortie according to aircraft energy planning and did not prepare the alternate route at all. Leg headings, leg times and the fuel checkpoints of the route were left undefined and the mission planning sheets were still incomplete at step-in. IP had to recompute the route fuel and impose a turnaround point on the ground before the sortie could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to a threat present in the minimum threat set but not identified during planning, did not take the forecast headwind on the outbound legs into consideration and left the alternate route unplanned. The planning sheets were brought to an acceptable state only after IP indicated each missing leg time and fuel figure in turn. The plan reached the lower limit of the requirement solely through verbal prompting and delayed step-in.
texts.2: SP, due to a currency shortfall that was not addressed at the start of the planning phase, first built an energy plan that did not cover the second leg of the route at the planned altitude. SP detected the shortfall while cross-checking the planning sheet against the Flight Manual and recomputed leg fuel, leg times and the alternate route before the brief, without IP intervention. The corrected plan covered the full route with the required reserve.
texts.3: SP planned the navigation sortie suitably, according to aircraft energy planning and own training level, taking into consideration all the data required for mission planning. Route legs, headings, leg times, fuel checkpoints and the alternate mission were computed correctly and the planning sheets were complete and legible before the brief. No figure required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP produced a navigation plan of exceptional quality, with leg times, fuel checkpoints and the alternate route computed to the minute and cross-checked against the Flight Manual and the Local Area Procedures. Every contingency raised during the brief was already supported by figures SP had prepared in advance. Deviations from the ideal plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP planned the sortie within standards, but the energy plan rested on the minimum route fuel with no usable reserve and the alternate mission was worked out in outline only. The trend is toward a plan that satisfies the requirement on paper while leaving no margin for a diversion or a delayed recovery. SP is expected to build the alternate route to the same level of detail as the primary one on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP planned the navigation sortie with IP naming the energy-planning factors to include and confirming the leg headings, times and fuel checkpoints alongside SP, due to this being the first full energy plan SP has built for an actual navigation sortie. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to compute more of the route legs independently, with IP confirming the fuel checkpoints, on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP planned the navigation sortie according to aircraft energy planning, with route legs, headings, leg times and fuel checkpoints computed correctly, due to the alternate route being worked out in outline before the primary route's reserve was confirmed against it, recognized only when the record was checked a second time. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the primary reserve before the alternate route is worked in outline on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP planned the navigation sortie according to aircraft energy planning, with route legs, headings, leg times and fuel checkpoints computed correctly, due to the alternate route being worked out in outline before the primary route's reserve was confirmed against it, caught during the routine cross-check that followed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to build the alternate route to the same detail as the primary as each is planned.
texts_at.3: SP planned the navigation sortie according to aircraft energy planning, with route legs, headings, leg times and fuel checkpoints computed correctly, due to the alternate route being worked out in outline before the primary route's reserve was confirmed against it, caught within the same step it occurred. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check the alternate route against the primary reserve in the same pass it is drafted.

texts_above.1: SP planned the navigation sortie according to aircraft energy planning, with route legs, headings, leg times and fuel checkpoints computed correctly. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP planned the navigation sortie suitably, with route legs, headings, leg times, fuel checkpoints and the alternate mission computed correctly and the planning sheets complete and legible before the brief. Carrying the alternate route to the same level of computed detail as the primary would remove the last soft spot in the plan. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good energy-plan discipline.
texts_above.3: SP produced planning sheets in which every leg, fuel checkpoint and the alternate mission were cross-checked against the Flight Manual, with no figure requiring correction by IP. The only refinement available was to compute the alternate route to the minute, as the primary route already was. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good energy-plan discipline.
texts_above.4: SP produced a navigation plan of exceptional quality, with leg times, fuel checkpoints and the alternate route computed to the minute and cross-checked against the Flight Manual and the Local Area Procedures, with every contingency raised at the brief already supported by prepared figures. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent energy-plan discipline.

error_modes.label: MISSION BRIEFING EXECUTION AND DECLARATION OF TRAINING HANDICAPS

texts.0: SP, due to preparation limited to reading the route on the map without rehearsing the briefing sequence, did not execute the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide and omitted the route, checkpoint and lost procedures paragraphs entirely. SP also did not inform IP of the navigation sorties missed earlier in the syllabus. IP had to stop the brief and personally deliver the missing items before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to a briefing board completed in the last minutes before the brief, covered the items out of the order of the Mission Briefing Guide and passed over the emergency and lost procedures paragraphs until IP called for them. The handicap in low level chart reading was declared only after direct questioning by IP. The brief reached the lower limit of the standard through repeated verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to the map and the planning sheet being laid out only at the briefing table, started the brief without the weather and NOTAM items in their proper sequence. SP recognized the omission at the end of the first paragraph, returned to the correct point of the Mission Briefing Guide and completed the remaining items in order, without IP intervention. Own training handicaps were declared unprompted.
texts.3: SP took part in and executed the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide, covering route, checkpoints, timings, weather, emergencies and lost procedures in the prescribed order. SP informed IP of the handicaps accumulated so far in training without being asked. The brief required no addition or correction by IP.
texts.4: SP delivered the mission briefing to an exceptional standard, following the Mission Briefing Guide item by item and supporting each route paragraph with the computed figures and the alternate mission. SP declared own training handicaps and proposed how the sortie would address them. Nothing of substance remained for IP to add.
texts.marginal: SP briefed within standards, but the route and checkpoint paragraphs were delivered from the planning sheet almost word for word, with little evidence that the picture had been built mentally. The trend is toward a brief that is complete in form but shallow in content, which will not support the higher navigation sorties. SP is expected to brief the route from the chart, without reading, on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP delivered the mission briefing with IP prompting the sequence of the Mission Briefing Guide and naming the training handicaps for SP to declare, due to this being the first briefing SP has delivered to this Guide's full sequence. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to deliver more of the briefing from the Guide's sequence independently, with IP prompting only the items still missing, and to declare training handicaps unprompted on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP took part in and executed the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide, covering route, checkpoints, weather, emergencies and lost procedures, due to one paragraph of the route review being read close to word for word from the planning sheet, caught only on a later review of the paperwork. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to brief the route from the chart rather than from the planning sheet on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP took part in and executed the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide, covering route, checkpoints, weather, emergencies and lost procedures, due to one paragraph of the route review being read close to word for word from the planning sheet, picked up during the next scheduled check. texts_at.3: SP took part in and executed the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide, covering route, checkpoints, weather, emergencies and lost procedures, due to one paragraph of the route review being read close to word for word from the planning sheet, noticed immediately and corrected in the same action. texts.0: SP, due to running the checks from memory in order to make the briefed taxi time, did not execute the checks according to the checklist and left the fuel quantity and the navigation equipment items unread. error_modes.label: COMPLETENESS OF THE LAP AND SOP GROUND SEQUENCE

texts.0: SP, due to an out of sequence ground flow built around the aircraft rather than around the published order, skipped procedures required by the Local Area Procedures and the SOPs, including the walk around of the external stores and the ground frequency check. The sortie could not have been released with the sequence as executed. IP had to intervene and impose the published order of the ground phase.
texts.1: SP, due to attention absorbed by an unrelated cockpit indication, omitted the arming and the pre taxi radio procedures of the SOPs and began the flow only after IP restated the published sequence. The remaining procedures were completed in the correct order but each transition required a verbal cue. The ground phase met the lower limit of the standard and ran past the briefed timeline.
texts.2: SP, due to a ground flow started before the aircraft documents had been reviewed, initially left out the acceptance procedure required by the Local Area Procedures. SP identified the gap while cross-checking the forms and executed the missing procedure before engine start, without IP intervention. The rest of the ground sequence followed the SOPs in the published order.
texts.3: SP did not skip any procedure required by the Local Area Procedures and the SOPs, and executed the normal ground procedures described in the Flight Manual in the published order. The documents, the acceptance and the pre taxi procedures were all completed. The ground phase was released without any addition by IP.
texts.4: SP executed the ground sequence to an exceptional standard, with every Local Area Procedure and SOP requirement completed in the published order and without a single prompt. SP also identified a discrepancy in the aircraft forms and resolved it with the ground crew before it could affect the timeline. Nothing in the sequence was left to be covered by IP.
texts.marginal: SP completed the ground sequence within standards, but the order was recovered rather than planned, with two procedures executed only after SP recognized they were about to be passed. The trend is toward a sequence that is complete at the end but not disciplined in its progress. SP is expected to follow the published order from the first item on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the ground sequence with IP naming each Local Area Procedure and SOP item in its published place, due to this being the first time SP has run the full published ground sequence for this aircraft. SP is expected to reach more of the published sequence independently, with IP checking for omissions, on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: GROUND CREW COORDINATION AND CLEARANCE BEFORE SWITCH OR CONTROL MOVEMENT

texts.0: SP, due to an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of the intended action, did not cooperate with the ground crew without allowing misapprehensions and moved the flight controls while the crew chief was still at the wing. SP was not aware of the ground crew position before activating the switch and no acknowledgement was obtained. IP had to intervene physically to stop the action.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to pass a required call at the briefed point, started the engine sequence with a hand signal that the ground crew read differently from the one intended. SP confirmed the crew position and the intention only after IP called for the acknowledgement. Coordination was restored at the lower limit of the standard and only through the verbal cue from the rear cockpit.
texts.2: SP, due to lack of communication of the recognized problem to the ground crew, initially began the control check without a clear signal that the area was clear. SP stopped the action on own initiative, established eye contact with the crew chief, obtained the acknowledgement and repeated the check correctly, without IP intervention. The remaining ground coordination was unambiguous.
texts.3: SP cooperated with the ground crew without allowing misapprehensions and was aware of the crew position before activating any switch or moving any aircraft control. Every signal was given clearly and acknowledged before the corresponding action. No coordination item required IP intervention.
texts.4: SP coordinated with the ground crew to an exceptional standard, confirming the position of every person around the aircraft before each switch and control movement and using unambiguous signals throughout. SP also anticipated the crew chief needs at the chocks and the fire guard position without being prompted. No misapprehension arose at any point of the ground phase.
texts.marginal: SP coordinated with the ground crew within standards, but two signals were given while looking inside the cockpit and the acknowledgement was assumed rather than seen. The trend is toward coordination that works because the crew chief compensates for it. SP is expected to confirm the acknowledgement visually before every switch and control movement on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the ground crew coordination with IP demonstrating the signal for each switch movement and confirming the crew chief's acknowledgement alongside SP, due to this being the first time SP has coordinated the full set of ground crew signals independently of a walk-through. SP is expected to give and confirm more of the signals independently, with IP checking the acknowledgement, on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: AIRCRAFT CONDITION ASSESSMENT, FLIGHT PERMISSIBILITY AND HANDLING OF LEVERS AND SWITCHES

texts.0: SP, due to a preflight inspection conducted without reference to the Flight Manual sequence, did not specify the aircraft condition correctly and declared it fit for flight with an open write up in the forms that affected the navigation equipment. SP also selected the wrong switch position for the transponder and the navigation radio during the cockpit check. IP had to reassess the aircraft condition and correct both selections before start.
texts.1: SP, due to the aircraft forms being reviewed after the walk around rather than before it, reached a decision on flight permissibility that was hesitant and was reversed twice. Two levers were placed in the correct position only after IP named them. The assessment and the switch selections met the lower limit of the standard through verbal prompting alone.
texts.2: SP, due to a walk around started from the wrong side of the aircraft, initially missed a fluid trace at the main gear and continued toward the cockpit. SP returned to the position on own initiative, examined it, discussed it with the ground crew and reached a correct and confident decision on flight permissibility, without IP intervention. All levers and switches were subsequently set correctly on the first attempt.
texts.3: SP specified the aircraft condition and decided its flight permissibility correctly and confidently, on the basis of the walk around and the aircraft forms. SP knew and used correctly all aircraft levers and switches during the ground phase. No assessment or selection required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP assessed the aircraft condition to an exceptional standard, correlating the walk around findings with the open entries in the forms and stating the flight permissibility decision with clear justification. Every lever and switch was identified and set correctly without hesitation and without a single misselection. The whole assessment stood without any input from IP.
texts.marginal: SP assessed the aircraft condition within standards, but the decision on flight permissibility was expressed tentatively and the selection of two less used switches required a visible search of the panel. The trend is toward knowledge that is adequate on the ground but will be slow under time pressure. SP is expected to state the permissibility decision without hesitation and to locate every switch by position on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: TAXI ROUTE COMPLIANCE, GROUND PATH CLEARANCE AND STOPPING

texts.0: SP, due to attention held on the kneeboard route card while the aircraft was moving, did not follow the specified taxi route and turned onto the parallel taxiway against the published direction. SP did not ensure that the ground path was clear of obstacles and allowed the aircraft to creep during the leak check. The stops were abrupt and oscillatory and IP had to take control to stop the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a taxi speed set too high for the turns of the published route, reached the holding point outside the specified line and stopped the aircraft with two clear oscillations of the nose. The correct route and the correct stopping point were established only after IP called the turn and the braking. Ground handling stayed at the lower limit of the standard throughout the taxi.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan concentrated ahead of the aircraft rather than along the whole ground path, initially began the turn toward the wrong taxiway intersection. SP recognized the divergence from the specified route, stopped the turn and rejoined the published route in time, without IP intervention. The aircraft was subsequently held stationary for the leak check and the line up without any movement.
texts.3: SP followed the specified taxi route and ensured that the ground path of the aircraft was clear of obstacles throughout the taxi. SP stopped the aircraft as required, without oscillations and without IP intervention, and allowed no aircraft movement when it had to be halted for the leak check and the line up. Taxi speed was appropriate for every turn.
texts.4: SP taxied to an exceptional standard, following the specified route precisely, clearing the ground path continuously on both sides and adjusting speed ahead of each turn. Every stop was smooth and on the required point, with no oscillation and no movement during the leak check and the line up. Nothing in the ground handling required comment from IP.
texts.marginal: SP taxied within standards, but the clearing scan was directed almost entirely ahead of the aircraft and the stops were achieved with late braking that produced a small nose movement. The trend is toward ground handling that is safe today only because the taxiway was uncongested. SP is expected to widen the clearing scan and to anticipate the braking point on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP taxied the specified route with IP naming each turn and the stopping points in advance, due to this being the first taxi SP has flown along this specific route without a walk-through beforehand. The Training Section introduces this task at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. error_modes.label: OFF STATION GROUND OPERATIONS: CHOCKS, PARKING BRAKE AND TRANSIENT SERVICING

texts.0: SP, due to an assumption that transient servicing at the intermediate field would match the home station, made no plan for absent servicing fluids or equipment and accepted a refuel that could not be verified. The aircraft was left on the parking brake with no chocks, and the home station was not contacted about the doubtful servicing. IP had to stop the servicing, arrange the chocks and make the coordination call.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the flight plan rather than on the actual transient facilities, asked for chocks and tie down ropes only after IP pointed at the ramp position and the forecast wind. The doubt over the servicing equipment was raised with the home station only when IP named the requirement. The off station handling reached an acceptable state through prompting alone.
texts.2: SP, due to the arrival paperwork at a civilian field not accustomed to military aircraft, initially left the aircraft on the parking brake without chocks. SP recognized that the parking brake system bleeds over time, obtained chocks from the transient crew and had the tie down ropes positioned for the forecast night wind, without IP intervention. The servicing continued only after the home station was contacted.
texts.3: SP treated the off station ground phase as a distinct problem, had the aircraft chocked rather than left on the parking brake alone and confirmed the transient servicing capability before accepting any fluid. Where doubt existed, the home station was contacted before the servicing continued. Nothing in the off station handling required IP intervention.
texts.4: SP managed the off station ground phase to an exceptional standard, briefing the transient crew on the propeller safety zone and on the servicing requirements of the aircraft before the paperwork began. The aircraft was chocked and, given the forecast night wind, tied down, and the home station was contacted over a fluid specification that could not be confirmed on the ramp. Every element of the turnaround was settled before the crew returned to the aircraft.

error_modes.label: CLEARANCE READBACK AND PROGRESSIVE TAXI AT AN UNFAMILIAR FIELD

texts.0: SP, due to an expectation that the clearance would mirror what was filed, read back the filed routing and squawk instead of the amended ones and did not query the difference. SP did not request progressive taxi instructions at the unfamiliar field, took the wrong turn out of the transient ramp and entered a taxiway not included in the clearance. IP had to take control, stop the aircraft and coordinate with ground.
texts.1: SP, due to listening for the expected words rather than to the instruction as given, read back the taxi clearance with two elements missing and accepted an amended departure frequency without confirming it. The complete readback and the request for progressive taxi followed prompts from IP in both cases. The ground phase remained at the lower limit of an acceptable standard up to the holding point.
texts.2: SP, due to a clearance delivered faster than it could be written down, initially read back an incorrect squawk and an incomplete taxi routing. SP recognized the uncertainty, asked ground to say again and then requested progressive taxi for the unfamiliar route, without IP intervention. The remaining instructions were read back complete and correct.
texts.3: SP read back every clearance in full, including the amendments to the filed routing and to the departure frequency, and confirmed anything that appeared different from standard. Where the taxi route at the unfamiliar field was not obvious, SP requested progressive taxi instructions before moving. No transmission or routing item required IP intervention.
texts.4: SP handled the ground radios to an exceptional standard, copying the clearance in a fixed order, reading back every element and querying the one item that differed from the filed flight plan before accepting it. SP requested progressive taxi for the unfamiliar transient ramp and confirmed each turn against the field chart before making it. Nothing in the readbacks or the ground routing gave IP anything to comment on.
texts.marginal: SP read back the clearances within standards, but two readbacks were built from what was expected rather than from what was written down, and the taxi route at the unfamiliar field was followed from memory of the chart instead of a progressive request. The trend is toward accepting a clearance that has already been amended. SP is expected to write the clearance before reading it back and to ask for progressive taxi when the route is not obvious on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: AFTER LANDING TAXI AND POST FLIGHT WALK AROUND AFTER THE NAVIGATION SORTIE

texts.0: SP, due to treating the sortie as complete at touchdown, proceeded back to the ramp across an active runway without obtaining clearance and taxied fast through the transient parking area. The post flight walk around was omitted entirely and a damaged main tire and a missing panel fastener were left unreported to maintenance. IP had to stop the aircraft at the runway hold line and carry out the post flight inspection.
texts.1: SP, due to attention already on the debrief, taxied back with a scan barely outside the cockpit and requested the crossing clearance only after IP called for it. The post flight walk around was carried out after a prompt, and the fluid trace on the wheel well fairing was reported to maintenance only when IP named it. Every item of the closing phase depended on IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the workload of the paperwork at the end of a long navigation sortie, initially started to step down from the wing without the over the rail check. SP stopped, verified the ejection and CFS pins, the ISS position, the battery and the OBOGS lever, then completed the post flight walk around and reported a bird strike mark to maintenance, without IP intervention. Nothing of the closing sequence was left undone.
texts.3: SP taxied after landing with the same caution used before takeoff, obtained clearance before crossing the active runway and completed the after landing and shutdown checklist items in full. The post flight walk around was carried out and the one abnormality found was reported to maintenance. The sortie was treated as complete only after the aircraft was parked and the engine shut down.
texts.4: SP closed the sortie to an exceptional standard, taxiing back with a full clearing scan, obtaining every crossing clearance and keeping sight of the ground personnel throughout the shutdown. The over the rail check was made deliberately before stepping down, and the walk around covered the wheel well, the speed brake and the engine bay areas. Both minor findings were written up and passed to maintenance with the aircraft forms.
texts.marginal: SP completed the after landing and post flight phase within standards, but the taxi back was flown with a noticeably relaxed scan and the walk around took well under the time needed to look at each area. The trend is toward a closing phase where the sortie is treated as over before the aircraft is parked. SP is expected to hold the same discipline until the last checklist item is complete on the next sortie.
